name: Gittensor

paragraphs: A Gittensor miner submits changes to approved open-source projects, reports issues that someone else fixes, or supplies a GPU server. For GitHub work, the project lists two CPU cores and 4 GB of RAM, and no server needs to stay online. When a validator, a participant that scores the miners' work, first accepts your fine-grained, read-only GitHub token, it binds that account to your registered wallet hotkey, the key a miner works with. GPU mining requires a supported card, 100 GB of free storage and a publicly reachable server that passes periodic checks.

When projects are funded, validators weigh code changes, and each project normally requires three qualifying merged pull requests and an 80% merge rate among merged and closed requests. Contributors share each pool in proportion to score, while an open request normally reserves 20% of its potential score in points. Scoring runs about every two hours and looks back 30 days by default, and the 12-hour grace period starts at merge.

The project describes earnings for this work, but at the reviewed commit the project list is empty and the GPU share is zero, so all miner emissions go to UID 0 for recycling. If you want to change GitHub accounts, the validator tells you to deregister and re-register. Read from https://github.com/entrius/gittensor/tree/main at commit 884ce17 on 2026-11-23.
mining_note.how_it_was_made: This note was put together by AI agents and not by a person who mines here. One agent read the subnet's public repository and wrote down what a miner does, what it takes and how the work is paid, with a source for each statement, and a second agent opened every source and took out whatever it did not support. Of 36 source checks, 21 held, 2 did not hold and 13 could not be opened, and only what held is in the text above. Nothing of the subnet's code was run, and the note describes the code as it stood on the day and at the commit named in its last sentence, so it can be out of date.
